purpose: Obinutuzumab is used to treat certain types of blood cancers, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and follicular lymphoma. It is often used in combination with other cancer medicines. Your doctor chose this medication to help slow or stop the growth of cancer cells in your body.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes proteins called antibodies that find and attack harmful things in your body. Obinutuzumab is a man-made antibody that seeks out a specific target called CD20, which sits on the surface of certain cancer cells. Once it attaches to those cells, it signals your immune system to destroy them, helping to reduce or eliminate the cancer.
common_side_effects: Infusion reactions (chills, fever, nausea, or low blood pressure during or shortly after your IV treatment), low blood cell counts (which can make you tired, increase infection risk, or cause easy bruising or bleeding), nausea, diarrhea, constipation, cough, and feeling very tired.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious infusion reactions, especially during your first treatment — you will be watched closely and given pre-medications to reduce this risk. It can significantly lower your white blood cell counts, raising your chance of serious infections, including a rare but dangerous brain infection called PML. It may reactivate hepatitis B in people who have had it before, so tell your doctor your full medical history. Avoid live vaccines while on this medicine. Tell your doctor right away if you have signs of infection like fever, chills, or unusual tiredness.
typical_dosing: Obinutuzumab is given as an IV infusion (through a vein) at a clinic or infusion center — you will not give this to yourself at home. For CLL, it is typically given over several months in cycles, starting with a split first dose. For follicular lymphoma, it follows a different schedule set by your doctor. Your care team will give you medicines before each infusion to help prevent reactions and will monitor you closely throughout your treatment.
